concept.body: Four statements from one 'If P, then Q': the CONVERSE swaps to 'If Q, then P'; the INVERSE negates both to 'If not P, then not Q'; the CONTRAPOSITIVE swaps AND negates to 'If not Q, then not P'. Only the contrapositive always shares the original's truth — the converse must be checked on its own.

explanationVariants: 'If Q, then P' swaps the two parts of 'If P, then Q' — that's the converse.
Swapping hypothesis and conclusion (no negation) is the converse.

widget.prompt: Which statement is the CONVERSE of "If it rains, the ground is wet"?

options.label: If the ground is wet, then it rains
options.feedback: Swap the parts: wet ground becomes the hypothesis — the converse.

options.label: If it does not rain, the ground is not wet
options.feedback: Both parts negated — that's the INVERSE, not the converse.

options.label: If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain
options.feedback: Swapped AND negated — that's the CONTRAPOSITIVE.

options.label: If it rains, the ground is wet
options.feedback: Unchanged — that's the original statement.

steps.body: Every theorem has a **converse** — its arrow reversed. Theorem: parallel lines ⇒ equal corresponding angles. Converse: equal corresponding angles ⇒ parallel lines. The converse is what makes the parallel-line CONSTRUCTION valid — copying an angle forces the lines parallel. But a converse must be proved separately; reversing an arrow doesn't guarantee truth.

widget.prompt: Theorem: "If lines are parallel, then alternate interior angles are equal." What is its CONVERSE?

options.label: If alternate interior angles are equal, then the lines are parallel
options.feedback: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion — equal angles become the assumption, parallel the result.

options.label: If lines are not parallel, then alternate interior angles are not equal
options.feedback: That's the INVERSE (both parts negated), not the converse. The converse swaps the two parts as-is.

options.label: If alternate interior angles are not equal, then the lines are not parallel
options.feedback: That's the CONTRAPOSITIVE (swap AND negate). The plain converse just swaps: equal angles ⇒ parallel.

options.label: If lines are parallel, then corresponding angles are equal
options.feedback: That's a different theorem entirely — not a rearrangement of this one's parts.

explanationVariants: A converse swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts. Original: parallel ⇒ equal angles. Converse: equal angles ⇒ parallel.
Reverse the arrow: the conclusion becomes the hypothesis and vice versa.

widget.prompt: How do you form the converse of "If P, then Q"?

options.label: Swap them: "If Q, then P"
options.feedback: The converse exchanges hypothesis and conclusion — Q becomes the assumption, P the result.

options.label: Negate both: "If not P, then not Q"
options.feedback: That's the INVERSE. The converse swaps the parts without negating them.

options.label: Swap and negate: "If not Q, then not P"
options.feedback: That's the CONTRAPOSITIVE. The converse only swaps — no negation.

options.label: Keep it the same: "If P, then Q"
options.feedback: That's the original statement unchanged. The converse reverses the arrow.

steps.body: A true statement's converse **need not be true.** "If it's a square, it's a rectangle" is true; its converse "if it's a rectangle, it's a square" is false. So each transversal converse is its own theorem — luckily, all of them ARE true for lines, which is what powers parallel constructions and proofs of parallelism.

widget.prompt: "If a number is divisible by 4, it is divisible by 2" is true. Is its CONVERSE ("if divisible by 2, then divisible by 4") also true?

options.label: No — 6 is divisible by 2 but not by 4
options.feedback: 6 is a counterexample: the converse fails, showing a true statement can have a false converse.

options.label: Yes — converses are always true
options.feedback: Converses are NOT automatically true. Here 6 (divisible by 2, not 4) breaks it.

options.label: Yes — because the original is true
options.feedback: The original's truth says nothing about the converse. 6 disproves this one.

options.label: It cannot be determined
options.feedback: It can — one counterexample (6) settles it: the converse is false.

predict.prompt: A TRUE theorem is about to meet its converse. Must the converse be true as well?

options.label: No — truth doesn't automatically flow backward
Yes — same facts, same truth

predict.reveal: 'Divisible by 4 ⇒ divisible by 2' is true, yet 6 is divisible by 2 and not by 4 — the reverse arrow fails. A statement and its converse are separate claims, and each direction must earn its own proof.

explanationVariants: The parallel construction copies an angle to make corresponding angles equal; the CONVERSE (equal corresponding ⇒ parallel) is what guarantees the result is actually parallel.
Building equal angles only proves parallelism because the converse licenses that direction.

widget.prompt: Why does the parallel-through-a-point construction actually produce a parallel line?

options.label: The CONVERSE of the corresponding-angles theorem: equal corresponding angles ⇒ parallel
options.feedback: Copying the angle makes corresponding angles equal; the converse turns that equality into a guarantee of parallelism.

options.label: The corresponding-angles theorem itself (parallel ⇒ equal angles)
options.feedback: That direction ASSUMES parallel to get equal angles — but the construction has equal angles and wants to CONCLUDE parallel. That's the converse.

options.label: Because the compass draws parallel lines directly
options.feedback: The compass draws arcs, not parallels — parallelism is EARNED through the equal-angle converse.

options.label: Because two points determine a line
options.feedback: That places the line but says nothing about its being parallel. The converse does that work.

steps.body: So the toolkit is symmetric. FORWARD (parallel ⇒ angle relationships) computes unknown angles when you know lines are parallel. BACKWARD, via the converses (angle relationships ⇒ parallel) proves lines parallel when you know the angles. Same facts, arrows both ways.

widget.prompt: You have measured the corresponding angles and found them equal. Turn the blue line until its angle matches the dark line's — and watch whether that alone is enough to force them parallel.
widget.successFeedback: Equal angles, and the lines are parallel — that is the CONVERSE doing the work, not the original theorem. The forward theorem starts from parallel and hands you equal angles; here you started from equal angles and got parallel. Same two facts, opposite arrows, and only the converse licenses this direction.
widget.angleFeedback: The angles still differ, so the lines still converge somewhere. Match the angle exactly — the converse needs EQUAL corresponding angles, not merely close ones.
widget.distanceFeedback: The direction is right. Sliding the line changes where it sits but never whether it is parallel — position is not what the converse is about.

hints: For the lines to be parallel, which relationship must the two co-interior angles satisfy?
Co-interior (same-side interior) angles must be SUPPLEMENTARY: (2x + 10) + 3x = 180.
explanationVariants: By the co-interior converse, the lines are parallel exactly when the same-side interior angles sum to 180°: (2x + 10) + 3x = 180 → 5x = 170 → x = 34.
Set the co-interior sum to 180 and solve: 5x + 10 = 180, x = 34.

widget.prompt: Two lines are cut by a transversal. The co-interior (same-side interior) angles are (2x + 10)° and (3x)°. What value of x forces the lines to be PARALLEL?

commonErrors.feedback: x = 10 comes from setting the angles EQUAL (2x+10 = 3x) — but co-interior angles are parallel when SUPPLEMENTARY, not equal. Solve (2x+10)+3x = 180: x = 34.
x = 38 solves 5x = 190 — a dropped +10. The equation is (2x+10)+3x = 180, i.e. 5x+10 = 180, so x = 34.

takeaways: A converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion — and needs its own proof.
A true statement can have a false converse; the transversal converses happen to be true.
Forward theorems compute angles from parallels; converses prove parallels from angles.
